inventory_audit.rationale: Read from the title page through Appendix B. Chapter 1 states RQ1-RQ3. Chapter 2 is background. Chapter 3 and Appendices A-B define the HSIS analysis and the simulation. Chapter 4 reports RQ1 (Table 4.1), RQ2 (Tables 4.2-4.7) and RQ3 (Tables 4.8-4.9, Figures 4.12-4.38); Chapter 5 draws the conclusions. HSIS results are entered as blocked claims, and the unreported power analysis as S8, rather than omitted.

claims.methods: Two engines. Chen's own seeded R code (Appendices A-B) was replayed exactly with R 4.1.3 and the 2021-08-02 package snapshot on an R-capable host (issues #92 and #118): the datasets her printed, seeded code generates are identical to her literal printed pipeline (largest difference 0), first 64,000 of them (50 replications per condition), then all 1,280,000 (1,000 per condition). This reproduces what her printed code produces; it is not necessarily the data behind her published results, which the h-absent analysis shows lacked the interaction wherever h > 0 (DISAGREEMENTS.yaml). Her bootstrap sets no seed, so the full simulation with 500 bootstrap resamples per analysis ran in an independent Python/NumPy re-implementation (validated against scikit-learn OLS and explicit resampling; the first run used Python without asking the person, who then agreed to keep it for the bootstrap, simulation/fallback.json); bootstrap-based agreement is judged on summaries. Chen's figures 4.12-4.38 were digitized: 4.12-4.16 exactly from the PDF drawing paths (reading error at most .002), 4.17-4.38 from images (reading errors up to about .02). Bias is the mean of 1,000 estimates minus the population value (PNDE = c', TNDE = c' + ah).
claims.uncertainty: Our largest |bias| over all 19,200 condition-cutoff-effect results is 0.016, far inside .10; Monte Carlo standard error of a mean of 1,000 estimates is at most 0.006 in any cell.
claims.multiplicity: Descriptive summary over the full grid; no tests.
claims.status_reason: Every direct-effect result in our run lies within [-.05, .05]. Her printed code, replayed over all 1,000 replications: largest condition-mean bias 0.017 (0% beyond .10); 5.3% of 19,200 cell biases beyond 1.96 Monte Carlo SEs and 0.14% beyond 3.29, as expected with no bias; her estimates and ours differ beyond 1.96 combined SEs in 5.3% of cells; median SD ratio 1.000; slope of estimated on true h 0.9998-1.0005 (results/r_full_comparison.json). Her digitized bias (Figures 4.12-4.16) is an almost exact function of the design with no dependence on n: MINT -0.998*ah; PNDE -1.466, -0.965, -0.446 times c' by cutoff plus about -0.928*h (results/bias_structure.csv). DISAGREEMENTS.yaml entries h-absent, population-values and pnde-definition give the competing explanations and tests.
claims.reconstruction_scope: full design, independent re-implementation, own seeds
limitations: Chen's step that compared estimates with population values is not printed; the mechanism is inferred from her digitized figures and tables (DISAGREEMENTS.yaml population-values: partly explained), not read from her code.

claims.status_reason: Coverage is close to nominal in every effect-cutoff row of our run, and misses fall on both sides of the interval at similar rates. Her digitized coverage of nonzero PNIE falls with n to a plateau of 0.25, 0.487 and 0.736 at cutoffs 1-3 (the control share under her code), with the truth above the interval in about the treated share; a wrong population value per condition would drive coverage toward 0 instead. claims.reconstruction_scope: full design, independent re-implementation, own seeds
limitations: Our run shows a small positive imbalance (the truth lies above the CI slightly more often than below it), two orders of magnitude smaller than Chen's; we did not investigate its cause.

Which per-case rule produced her population values is not determined: one rule fits cutoffs 1-2 but not cutoff 3 exactly, and a step written for her text's reversed cutoff labels predicts the same plateau.

Every Type I error and power statement in Chapter 4 that names cells and a checkable outcome is tested on every cell set it names (simulation/statement_checks.py), with rates averaged over the factors it does not name, as in Chen's figures, and with fixed numeric readings of her words (for example "near zero" Type I < .025, "close to zero" power < .10, "around .80" .70-.90). A second reading moves every threshold .01 in her favour.
claims.uncertainty: With 1,000 replications, a cell coverage near .95 has a binomial standard error of about .007 and a rejection rate near .05 about .007. Chen reports no Monte Carlo error.
claims.multiplicity: 18 statements, each judged at its own threshold; no correction (descriptive).
claims.status_reason: 13 of 18 Type I statements agree (14 with slack). As a consistency check, every statement was also read on our cells with h replaced by 0 (other factors unchanged; the verdict_if_h_were_0 column). Then 39 of 46 statements hold, against 29 as designed; 10 of the 15 statements that disagree under both readings become agreements, and none that agrees becomes a disagreement. With h = 0, 7 statements still disagree under the strict reading: 10, 11, 30, 41, 44 (which disagree under both readings) and 2, 43 (which agree with the .01 slack) (the number column of results/statement_checks.csv). Chen also defines PNDE as "adding c' and h" (printed p. 104), whereas with the mediator intercept zero in her data-generating model the population PNDE is c'. Her digitized Figures 4.17-4.28 match our rates read with h = 0 at 79.1-100.0% of points per figure (at 4.3-100.0% with h as designed; results/rates_agreement.csv), and each statement was also read against her own figure points (verdict_on_chen_figures). Together with the exact replay of her code, which recovers h, this indicates that the data behind her results contained no interaction (an inference from her outputs; her code and data for those runs are not available) (DISAGREEMENTS.yaml h-absent). The remaining disagreements are threshold cases, her text against her own figures, and one TNDE cell set explained by her particular random draws (DISAGREEMENTS.yaml threshold-noise, prose-versus-own-figure, tnde-power-gap). The robust disagreements are MINT with a = 0, where ours is below Bradley's range at h = .05 through n = 5,000 (at most .019) and at h = .15 at n = 500 (.014-.020), as Chen reports, but about .05 at h = .34 and at h = .15 from n = 2,500 (.026-.033 at n = 1,000), whereas she reports no variation across h; and TNIE Type I statements with a = 0 at small n (statements 9, 10, 11), where our rates and her description fall on different sides of the robustness bounds. Read with h = 0, statements 9, 18 would hold in our run.
limitations: The numeric readings of Chen's words are ours; the slack column shows which verdicts depend on them.
Figures 4.17-4.21 were read from images; points hidden by another series are excluded from verdicts.

Chen's figures 4.12-4.38 were digitized: 4.12-4.16 exactly from the PDF drawing paths (reading error at most .002), 4.17-4.38 from images (reading errors up to about .02). Every Type I error and power statement in Chapter 4 that names cells and a checkable outcome is tested on every cell set it names (simulation/statement_checks.py), with rates averaged over the factors it does not name, as in Chen's figures, and with fixed numeric readings of her words (for example "near zero" Type I < .025, "close to zero" power < .10, "around .80" .70-.90). A second reading moves every threshold .01 in her favour.
claims.uncertainty: With 1,000 replications, a cell coverage near .95 has a binomial standard error of about .007 and a rejection rate near .05 about .007. Chen reports no Monte Carlo error.
claims.status_reason: 16 of 28 power statements agree (17 with slack): all 6 PNIE statements and all 5 PNDE statements agree; the disagreements concern TNIE, TNDE and MINT. As a consistency check, every statement was also read on our cells with h replaced by 0 (other factors unchanged; the verdict_if_h_were_0 column). Then 39 of 46 statements hold, against 29 as designed; 10 of the 15 statements that disagree under both readings become agreements, and none that agrees becomes a disagreement. With h = 0, 7 statements still disagree under the strict reading: 10, 11, 30, 41, 44 (which disagree under both readings) and 2, 43 (which agree with the .01 slack) (the number column of results/statement_checks.csv). Chen also defines PNDE as "adding c' and h" (printed p. 104), whereas with the mediator intercept zero in her data-generating model the population PNDE is c'. Her digitized Figures 4.17-4.28 match our rates read with h = 0 at 79.1-100.0% of points per figure (at 4.3-100.0% with h as designed; results/rates_agreement.csv), and each statement was also read against her own figure points (verdict_on_chen_figures). Together with the exact replay of her code, which recovers h, this indicates that the data behind her results contained no interaction (an inference from her outputs; her code and data for those runs are not available) (DISAGREEMENTS.yaml h-absent). The remaining disagreements are threshold cases, her text against her own figures, and one TNDE cell set explained by her particular random draws (DISAGREEMENTS.yaml threshold-noise, prose-versus-own-figure, tnde-power-gap).
limitations: Figures 4.22-4.28 were read from images; points hidden by another series are excluded from verdicts.

synthesis: Not replicated on the simulation headlines. Over all 3,840 condition-cutoff cells, every effect is unbiased (largest |bias| 0.016) and percentile-bootstrap coverage averages 95.0%, against Chen's 6-87% non-bias and 24-84% coverage; MINT power reaches 0.84 at n = 500 for the largest interaction, where Chen reports near zero. Of her 46 testable Type I and power statements, 29 agree (31 with .01 threshold slack), and 39 would hold in our run if h were 0. The n = 5,000 recommendation holds for most but not all cells. RQ2 is blocked by data access. Her printed, seeded R code, replayed exactly on all 1,280,000 datasets it generates, behaves like our run, so the disagreements arise in steps or runs she did not print: her digitized figures show results computed from data without the interaction h and population values wrong for one group of cases. Of 10 disagreements (DISAGREEMENTS.yaml), 8 are explained, 2 partly explained and 0 unexplained.
limitations: The bootstrap-based results (coverage, Type I error, power) come from the Python run with our own seeds; Chen's bootstrap is unseeded, so they agree with hers on summaries only. The R replay reproduces exactly the datasets and point estimates her printed, seeded code generates (all 1,000 replications per condition); her published results came from data without the interaction wherever h > 0, which the printed code does not produce, so the replay is not her published runs (H1-H4, S1-S3).

Chen's aggregation code, population values and result files are not printed. The mechanisms behind her bias, coverage and MINT results are inferred from her digitized figures and printed tables; they reproduce her patterns but are not read from her code (H1, H2, H3, S1).

Figures 4.17-4.38 were read from images (reading errors up to about .02 on rates); points hidden behind another series are not readings: digitized_rates.csv fills them in from the visible series (status occluded) and they are not used for statement verdicts, figure-agreement rates or E4 (H3, S2, S3).
RQ2 (HSIS) cannot be rerun: the restricted-use data are not available to this project (S4, S6); only the printed arithmetic and identities were checked (S5).
The announced power analysis by the SD of Y is not reported, so it cannot be assessed (S8).

The dissertation labels the cutoffs inconsistently: the code's index 1 is the 25th percentile (75% treated), while Chapter 3, the Table 4.8 note and her Head Start analysis have treatment below the cutoff; we report by the code (H1, H2).

Chen suggests global estimation with an incorrect functional form as a plausible explanation of the bias; in her data-generating model the assignment variable does not enter M or Y, so the fitted linear models are correctly specified (H1).
